subject: nuclear pacemaker
title: What If Your Heart Ran on Plutonium? In the 1970s, Thousands Did

scenes.text: What if the device keeping your heart beating ran on plutonium? For thousands of people, it did.
April 1970, Paris. A 58-year-old woman receives the first nuclear pacemaker: 150 milligrams of plutonium-238 in a sealed capsule.
Plutonium-238 decays and gets hot. The heat becomes a trickle of electricity. Half-life: 88 years. Ordinary pacemaker batteries then lasted about 30 months.
Estimates range from 1,400 to more than 3,000 implanted through the 70s and 80s. One woman fitted in 1973 still had hers running in 2007: 34 years.
The catch: when the patient dies, the device must be removed and shipped to Los Alamos National Laboratory. The plutonium is still government property.
Lithium batteries won. By 2003 fewer than 100 Americans still carried a nuclear heart. A few may be ticking today.

description:
What if your pacemaker ran on plutonium? From April 1970, when a 58-year-old woman in Paris received the first one, until the mid-1980s, pacemakers powered by the heat of decaying plutonium-238 were implanted in somewhere between about 1,400 and more than 3,000 patients, at a time when ordinary batteries lasted about 30 months.
The isotope's 88-year half-life meant some units ran for decades; one implanted in 1973 was still working in 2007. The devices are licensed nuclear sources: after death they must be removed and returned to Los Alamos National Laboratory. By 2003 an estimated 50 to 100 Americans still had one.

first_comment: The titanium capsule was built to survive a gunshot and a cremation furnace. Would you accept a power source that outlives you inside your chest?
